title: Small structures. Big impact!
content:
Scientific advances have enabled technologies that manipulate the total wavefunction of molecular systems through controlled confinement, thereby altering their physical, chemical, optical, and electronic properties. Despite these breakthroughs, our understanding of how to precisely control matter at the quantum level remains in its early stages. The confinement of molecular systems is a pervasive phenomenon across chemistry, physics, biology, astrochemistry, and engineering.

The COSY COST Action, Confined molecular systems: from a new generation of materials to the stars aimed to advance the understanding and control of confined molecular systems and to translate the resulting knowledge into practical applications.

These efforts range from developing new materials, including biomaterials with strong potential for industrial use, to understanding the chemistry behind molecular processes in space. To achieve these goals, COSY combined advanced experimental techniques for synthesising and characterising new nanomaterials with state-of-the-art theoretical modelling.

title: Giving a voice to Europe’s mountain communities
content:
Europe’s mountains cover almost 40% of the continent and are home to 17% of its population. Yet many mountain communities remain on the margins, facing limited economic opportunities, depopulation and exclusion from decisions that shape their futures.

For four years, the COST Action ‘A European forum for revitalisation of marginalised mountain areas’ (MARGISTAR) brought together more than 200 scientists, policymakers and local stakeholders from over 30 countries to explore how these communities could overcome isolation and build more sustainable futures.

“It was a journey of discovery,” says Professor Juha Hiedanpää of the Natural Resources Institute Finland (Luke), Chair of MARGISTAR. “We explored the natural, environmental, social and economic relationships that shape marginalised mountain areas and worked together to imagine practical solutions for their communities.”

title: Supporting the next generation of researchers: from ambition to action
content:
At the final conference of the COST Cross-Cutting Activity (CCA) on supporting the career development of young researchers, held on 28–29 October 2026 in Brussels, COST brought together 70 researchers, research organisations, career development experts and European stakeholders to exchange insights and reflect on the achievements of this CCA network.

How can Europe make research careers more attractive, sustainable and rewarding?
And what needs to change to ensure that early-career researchers have the support and opportunities they need to thrive?

Over the past two years, this CCA has explored some of the key challenges shaping research careers across Europe. Bringing together more than 50 members from 21 countries, it mobilised a diverse network of young researchers and career development experts across four dedicated working groups to explore the barriers, identify shared priorities and shape the future of research careers in Europe. The network has produced an impressive set of deliverables, which are all available in the dedicated CCA community on Zenodo.

title: Consistent rise in the number of COST proposals
content:
Yesterday 28 October, we closed the call for new COST Action proposals (OC-2026-1). Interim analysis shows the following:

  • The highest number of proposals ever submitted to a COST Open Call, with a 27% increase compared to OC-2025.
  • All 42 COST Member Countries participated in this call as Main Proposers. Italy had the most Main Proposers, followed by the United Kingdom and Spain.
  • Over 68,000 Main and Secondary Proposers participated, which is a 33.8% increase compared to the previous call.
  • 60% of the proposals cover two or more main fields of science, which is a 5% increase compared to OC-2025.
  • 33% of Main Proposers are affiliated with institutions in Inclusiveness Target Countries (ITCs), which is a 2% increase compared to OC-2025.

    • The proposals will now undergo evaluation. Up to 80 COST Actions will be approved in May 2027.

    If you are interested in applying for future network funding, you will soon be informed about our next Open Call 2027.

title: How a COST Innovators Grant helped build the Global Tsunami Model
content: Tsunamis are triggered by sudden events that displace large volumes of water. They are long waves that most frequently originate from earthquakes, setting the entire water column in motion, allowing the tsunami to propagate far from the source, in some cases, travelling entire oceans before striking land with potentially devastating force.

title: Connecting talent, knowledge and ideas. The power of research networks!
content:
On 22 October 2026, more than 100 researchers, policymakers, high-level speakers, experts, and other stakeholders from across Europe gathered at the COST Conference in Brussels to explore the latest developments shaping the future of European research and innovation, with a focus on the European Research Area (ERA) and the next Framework Programme (FP10).

At this decisive turning point for European research policy, research networks can drive scientific excellence, strengthen Europe’s global competitiveness and accelerate its capacity to innovate. This set the tone for the event, which was opened by COST President, Prof. Åse Gornitzka:

“Today’s conference raises an important question: what role can research networks play in shaping Europe’s future research and innovation landscape?

For over 50 years, COST has brought researchers together across countries, disciplines and career stages, creating opportunities to exchange ideas, build trust and turn shared scientific interests into lasting collaborations.

title: The future of early cancer detection with metamaterial technology and artificial intelligence
content:
Early detection and effective treatment of cancer are critical to improving patient survival outcomes. The rapid advancement of machine learning (ML), particularly deep learning, has led to significant improvements in the accuracy and efficiency of cancer screening, detection, and monitoring.

However, despite these advances, ML-based approaches face a significant limitation: the substantial computational resources required for the analysis and interpretation of medical images.

Detecting cancer at the earliest possible stage gives patients the best chance of successful treatment. Early diagnosis improves outcomes by enabling timely access to care and is therefore a critical public health strategy in all settings.

title: ODIN and BAANG for safer, greener skies
content:
Every time an aircraft takes off, thousands of structural components must work perfectly under stress, vibration and changing temperatures. Ensuring that these structures remain safe for decades is one of the greatest challenges in aviation. The COST Action Optimising Design for Inspection (ODIN) decided to rethink this challenge from the very beginning.

Instead of asking how aircraft should be inspected after they are built, ODIN focused on embedding inspection into the design itself. The idea is similar to the human nervous system. Just as your body feels pain and reacts early, ODIN worked on aircraft structures that can ‘feel’ damage and report it before it becomes serious.

As Action Chair, Dr Rhys Pullin, from Cardiff University, explains:

“Much like the human body’s nervous system, these ‘built-in senses’ will provide real-time updates on the health and safety of the aircraft. They’ll also help the plane automatically adjust its shape to improve fuel efficiency, make the ride smoother, and ensure everything is running at its best.”

Planes are struck by lightning about once a year, but this is always safe

title: From overlooked disease to global research priority
content:
Every October, Breast Cancer Awareness Month brings people around the world together under the pink ribbon to raise awareness, encourage early detection, support patients and fund research.

To mark this year’s campaign, COST is publishing a success story about the LOBSTERPOT Action on lobular breast cancer. The aim of this research initiative is to improve the detection, treatment and outcomes for patients.

For years, invasive lobular cancer (ILC) was one of the least understood forms of breast cancer. Despite being the second most common type, research efforts were scattered and coordinated clinical approaches were limited.

To change this, the COST Action Lobular Breast Cancer: Discovery Science, Translational Goals, Clinical Impact (LOBSTERPOT) brought together researchers, clinicians, and patient advocates, establishing one of the world’s leading scientific communities dedicated to this disease. In the process, the network has launched new clinical trials, developed diagnostic guidance that could influence future global standards, and transformed the way ILC is studied and understood.
